query: For phosphorus-containing high-entropy or compositionally complex alloys, what single intervention could improve glass-forming ability and the thermal stability of the amorphous state? Formulate one testable hypothesis that specifies the intervention without presupposing its class, the mechanism by which it would act, the predicted improvement relative to an otherwise comparable baseline, the conditions under which it should or should not work, supporting prior evidence, and an experiment whose result would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Implementing an ultra‐rapid quenching process (e.g., melt‐spinning achieving cooling rates on the order of 10^5–10^6 K/s) on phosphorus‐containing high‐entropy alloys will enhance their glass‐forming ability and yield an amorphous state with improved thermal stability compared to samples processed by slower cooling methods.
generation.material_initial_state: A molten phosphorus-containing high-entropy or compositionally complex alloy that contains elements such as Cr, Mn, Fe, Co, Ni (with phosphorus addition) and is prone to crystallization under slower cooling.
generation.intervention: Employing ultra-rapid quenching (using techniques such as melt-spinning) to achieve extremely high cooling rates.
generation.conditions: The intervention should be applied during solidification under an inert atmosphere and with controlled melt conditions; the effect is expected when the cooling rate exceeds the critical threshold (on the order of 10^5 K/s) but may not be observed if the cooling rate is significantly lower.
generation.structural_mediator: Enhanced undercooling that suppresses atomic diffusion and nucleation, leading to a more homogeneous amorphous structure with reduced microstructural heterogeneity.
generation.mechanism: Ultra-rapid cooling minimizes the time available for atoms to rearrange into crystalline phases; the high phosphorus content further disrupts nucleation, so that together they prevent crystallization and lock in a stable amorphous configuration that withstands thermal perturbations.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to slower-cooled samples (e.g., those cooled at ~50–3000 K/s), the ultra-rapidly quenched alloy will show a higher fraction of the amorphous phase and exhibit an increased crystallization onset temperature (i.e., improved thermal stability) as measured by techniques such as DSC, XRD, and TEM.
generation.baseline: Phosphorus-containing high-entropy alloys processed via conventional or moderately accelerated cooling rates that result in mixed crystalline/amorphous microstructures with lower crystallization onset temperatures.
generation.boundary: This hypothesis is expected to hold for alloys with compositions similar to Cr16Mn16Fe16Co16Ni16P20 and related systems; variations in phosphorus content or the overall elemental makeup might modulate the critical cooling rate or the magnitude of the improvement.
generation.uncertainty: The exact cooling rate threshold and the quantitative improvement in thermal stability are uncertain and may depend on the specific alloy composition, processing apparatus, and environmental conditions.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare a set of identical phosphorus-containing high-entropy alloy samples and solidify them under three different cooling conditions: slow cooling (e.g., ~50–3000 K/s), and ultra-rapid quenching via melt-spinning (e.g., ~10^5–10^6 K/s). Characterize each sample using X-ray diffraction (XRD) for phase identification, transmission electron microscopy (TEM) for microstructural analysis, and differential scanning calorimetry (DSC) to determine crystallization onset temperatures.
measurements: Fraction of amorphous phase as indicated by the broadness of XRD peaks and TEM imaging.
Crystallization onset temperature and thermal stability as measured by DSC.
Comparison of microstructural homogeneity across different cooling rates.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the ultra-rapidly quenched samples do not exhibit a statistically significant higher amorphous phase fraction and a measurable increase in crystallization onset temperature compared to the slower-cooled samples, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: This study investigates the influence of cooling rates on the microstructure and phase transformations of the high-entropy alloy Cr16Mn16Fe16Co16Ni16P20. The alloy was synthesized via arc melting and subjected to three cooling conditions: slow cooling (52 K/s), accelerated cooling after a short electric arc pulse (3018 K/s), and rapid quenching (10⁵–10⁶ K/s) using the melt-spinning method. The microstructures were characterized using X-ray diffraction (XRD), scanning electron microscopy (SEM), transmission electron microscopy (TEM), and Mössbauer spectroscopy. The thermal properties and phase transformations were analyzed using differential scanning calorimetry (DSC) and thermography. Slow cooling produced a complex crystalline microstructure, while accelerated cooling resulted in fewer phases. Rapid cooling yielded an amorphous structure, demonstrating that phosphorus and high mixing entropy enhance glass-forming ability. Phase transformations exhibited significant undercooling under accelerated cooling, with FCC phase crystallization shifting from 1706 K (slow cooling) to 1341 K, and eutectic crystallization from 1206 K to 960 K. This study bridges this gap, providing insights into the mechanisms of amorphization and phase transformation influenced by rapid cooling rates. This study focuses on the high-entropy alloy Cr16Mn16Fe16Co16Ni16P20, selected for its anticipated amorphization potential resulting from high configurational entropy and phosphorus addition. The cooling rates were systematically varied, with slow cooling averaging approximately 52 K/s, accelerated cooling at 3018 K/s, and melt-spinning achieving rapid cooling rates in the range of 10⁵–10⁶ K/s. We investigated the alloy’s phase transformations and microstructural evolution under different cooling conditions, including slow cooling on a copper plate, accelerated cooling after remelting, and rapid quenching using melt-spinning. By characterizing the resulting structures using XRD, SEM, TEM, and Mössbauer spectroscopy, we aim to advance the understanding of processing-condition effects on phase stability and amorphization in phosphorus-enriched HEAs, providing insights for the development of HEAs with tailored properties.
